Some of these advanced chemistries and designs could offer a more reliable supply of batteries and reduced costs by using alternatives to critical minerals, including lithium and graphite. These battery advancements include solid-state batteries (SSBs), lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, sodium-ion (Na-ion) batteries, vanadium redox flow batteries, lithium-titanate (LTO) batteries, and silicon (Si) anodes. Some battery options are commercially available, though most are still being optimized for capacity, performance, and cost-competitiveness. According to National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) experts, these are expected to be commercially available by 2030 or 2035. Some batteries are well suited for electric vehicle (EV) applications because of their reduced weight combined with their increased energy storage and faster charging, properties that are well suited for improved mobility. A leading example is Li-S, which uses abundant sulfur as the cathode material instead of critical minerals (Benveniste et al. 2018); it has been identified as useful for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), high-altitude pseudo-satellites, autonomous underwater vehicles, and heavy road vehicles (Dorfler et al. 2020). Relatively heavier-weight advanced batteries might be more suitable for stationary storage while offering improved performance, including Na-ion, redox flow, and the commercially available LTO. 73 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
